title: Sahih al-Bukhari
hookLine: a book that opens with intention, built from reports al-Bukhari judged sound

cards: Actions are judged by intentions, and each person gets what they intended. You traced those words through their chain a week ago. Now look at where they sit.
Open Sahih al-Bukhari to its first page, and that's where it begins: a report from Umar ibn al-Khattab that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said those words.
Before a single ruling about prayer, or fasting, or buying and selling, the reader meets a quiet question. Why are you here, opening this book? All that checking had to end up somewhere.
One of the places it ended up is today's word. Sahih al-Bukhari.

teach.b: You met al-Bukhari's journey long ago. Today, his book. Sahih means sound, healthy, whole: the top of the scale.
Al-Bukhari is the man, Muhammad ibn Isma'il, called after Bukhara, the city he came from. People often just call his book the Sahih, the sound one.

The sifting: tradition says al-Bukhari heard a vast number of reports on his travels and kept only a small share, the ones whose chains passed his test, each narrator trustworthy and careful, each known to have heard from the person before him.
Tradition also says that before writing each hadith into the book, he washed and prayed. Whether every detail of that story is exact or not, it shows what the book meant to the people who told it.
The headings: al-Bukhari set the reports under chapter titles he wrote himself, and those titles are often small arguments. A heading states a point, and the hadith beneath it back the point up.

teach.h: HIS UNDERSTANDING IS IN HIS HEADINGS.
teach.b: Scholars have a saying that al-Bukhari's understanding is in his headings. So the book isn't only a store of reports. It's also one careful reader's reading of them.
The place it holds: in Sunni scholarship, this book holds a special trust, and with tomorrow's book it makes up the pair called the two Sahihs.

Some communities gather to read it aloud, cover to cover, and celebrate when they finish. Shia Muslims have their own collections and their own science of grading, which this path reaches in a few days.
And remember where it starts. Before the rulings, the question of intention.

how: Sunni Muslims study Sahih al-Bukhari with teachers, cite its hadith by number, and in some communities gather to read it aloud from beginning to end.

o: at the chapter heading he set it under.

practice: Here's a hadith from its book of good manners, in plain words: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should say something good, or keep quiet.

Say it once, slowly, then think of the conversations ahead of you, at work, at home, in a group chat that's already buzzing. Find the one place where the second half would help most, keep quiet, and hold that place in mind.
